analysis.one_liner: Makes it much harder to sue landlords for housing discrimination and shields newspapers from discriminatory-ad liability.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Judiciary Committee: it drew zero cosponsors, went no further than a subcommittee referral, and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the Fair Housing Act to make discrimination cases far harder to bring and win. Only people who could prove they actually intended and were able to rent a particular dwelling could sue — which would bar civil rights "testers" who pose as renters to catch discrimination. Claims would need proof of intentional discrimination, newspapers would be immune from liability over discriminatory housing ads, and courts would be required to make the losing side pay legal costs, so a renter who lost a case would owe the landlord's legal fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Landlords accused of housing discrimination would gain three separate shields: suits by testers would be barred, claims would need proof of deliberate intent rather than showing a practice had a discriminatory effect, and prevailing landlords could automatically collect their legal costs. Newspaper and other publishers would gain immunity from liability for discriminatory housing advertisements they print. Fair-housing enforcement organizations, whose core method is sending testers, would lose their main courtroom tool.

how_it_helps.text: Bars lawsuits by anyone who cannot show, if the landlord asks, that they have the ability and intent to actually live in the dwelling — eliminating suits by fair-housing testers, the enforcement method most fair-housing groups rely on.

Requires that a discriminatory housing practice be 'committed with the intent to discriminate,' letting landlords escape liability for policies that exclude protected groups in effect even without a provable discriminatory purpose.
Grants newspapers and other publishers immunity from Fair Housing Act liability for discriminatory housing ads, so long as they reasonably relied on the advertising copy submitted to them.

Changes the fee rule so courts must award legal costs to whichever party prevails, meaning a renter who loses a discrimination suit would automatically owe the landlord's legal fees — a risk that would deter many valid claims.

analysis.who_pays: Renters who face discrimination would bear the cost, losing tester-based enforcement, having to prove deliberate intent, and risking an automatic award of the landlord's legal fees if their case failed. Fair-housing organizations would lose their principal enforcement method and face the same fee risk. People harmed by discriminatory housing advertising would have no claim against the paper that ran the ad.
analysis.who_pays_short: Renters facing discrimination and fair-housing groups

drawbacks.text: Testing — sending matched pairs of renters to see who gets shown a unit — is the main way housing discrimination is documented, because individual victims rarely can prove intent. Bar tester suits and much discrimination becomes effectively unenforceable in court.

Requiring proof of intentional discrimination would eliminate claims based on practices that have a discriminatory effect — for example, occupancy rules or screening criteria that exclude families with children or minority applicants without any stated discriminatory purpose.
Publishers could run housing ads that say things like 'whites only' without any liability, removing a check on discriminatory advertising in the rental market.

Mandatory fee-shifting cuts both ways in theory, but because discrimination cases are hard to prove, the practical effect would fall on victims: losing plaintiffs would automatically owe the prevailing landlord's costs, chilling suits by renters with real but hard-to-prove claims.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill responded to real, narrow grievances: some suits were filed by testers with no intention of renting, and publishers argued they should not answer for ad copy submitted in good faith. But the remedy went far beyond those problems. Requiring intent, barring tester suits, immunizing ad publishers, and mandating fee awards against losing plaintiffs together would have dismantled the enforcement tools the Fair Housing Act depends on, and the burden would fall on renters — disproportionately minority renters and families — who face discrimination. The cost to enforcement clearly outweighed the litigation-abuse concerns it addressed.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jon Fox of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on September 27, 1996, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
A week later, on October 4, 1996, it was sent to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution — the last action it ever received.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor, and the committee never held a markup or brought the bill to the floor.
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill died there.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Renters and fair-housing organizations are better off: the full set of Fair Housing Act enforcement tools — including tester suits, effect-based claims, and publisher liability — remained intact because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Jon D. Fox
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor; no colleague cosponsored it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair Henry Hyde)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over civil rights legislation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; after a single referral to the Constitution Subcommittee, it took no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican sponsored the bill, it drew zero cosponsors from either party, and no vote was ever held, so no partisan pattern ever emerged.

industries.note: The bill would have given landlords three shields against discrimination suits: a bar on tester plaintiffs, a requirement to prove deliberate intent, and automatic fee awards against losing tenants. Their gain would come directly out of renters' ability to enforce their housing rights.

The bill would have immunized publishers from Fair Housing Act liability for discriminatory housing ads they print in reasonable reliance on submitted copy. The benefit to publishers comes at the cost of leaving discriminatory advertising unpoliced.

Tester-based enforcement is how these groups document discrimination, and the bill would have barred testers from suing while exposing losing plaintiffs to mandatory fee awards. Their loss is the public's loss, since they act as the private enforcement arm of fair-housing law.
